title: Lost Memoir by Hiroshima Survivor Published 81 Years After the Atomic Bomb
excerpt: Kiyoshi Tanimoto's 230-page eyewitness account, discovered in a Yale University archive, is released on the 81st anniversary of the Hiroshima bombing — with a film adaptation already in production.
body:
• Kiyoshi Tanimoto's 230-page eyewitness memoir of the Hiroshima bombing, written in 1947, has been published for the first time after being discovered in Yale University's Beinecke Library.
  • The book, "Hiroshima, 8:15: The Lost Memoir," was released on August 6, 2026 — the 81st anniversary of the bombing — by Penguin Random House after a competitive three-way auction.
  • Tanimoto's daughter Koko Kondo, now 81 and a lifelong peace activist, wrote a 9,000-word foreword to the memoir.
  • A feature film adaptation is in pre-production, with Japanese actor Takehiro Hira set to play Tanimoto and filming scheduled for February 2027.

On the morning of August 6, 1945, Methodist minister Kiyoshi Tanimoto was transporting a handcart of belongings to a house in the Hiroshima suburb of Koi, roughly two miles from the city centre. He had slept poorly — air-raid warnings disrupted the night — and arrived at his destination at precisely 8:15 a.m., the moment the atomic bomb "Little Boy" detonated overhead, killing more than 60,000 people instantly.

Tanimoto survived. In the weeks and months that followed, he filled 230 pages with precise, brutal descriptions of what he witnessed — a manuscript that lay forgotten for nearly eight decades before being rediscovered in a U.S. university archive. That memoir, "Hiroshima, 8:15: The Lost Memoir," has now been published for the first time, released on the 81st anniversary of the bombing.

A Manuscript Lost and Found

Tanimoto wrote his account in English in 1947, two years after the bombing. The manuscript ended up among the papers of American journalist John Hersey, who had featured Tanimoto as one of six survivors in his landmark 1946 New Yorker article "Hiroshima" — a piece that became one of the most important works of journalism in the 20th century.

The memoir was found in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library at Yale University by Hersey's grandson, Cannon Hersey. It had sat unread among Hersey's archived papers for decades.

"Skin from faces, hands, arms, and breasts was stripped off or hanging loose. People were moving... without expression... following one after another in silence... like a procession of ghosts. Everything was beyond their comprehension."

— Kiyoshi Tanimoto, from "Hiroshima, 8:15"

The Weight of an Eyewitness

Tanimoto's account differs from Hersey's celebrated work in a crucial way: it is told entirely in the survivor's own voice, without journalistic mediation. He describes returning to Hiroshima's ruins to find "the whole city covered with dark clouds, and conflagrations breaking out in various directions," as "black drops of rain, as big as blackberries, began to fall — rain caused by the atomic bomb."

The book was acquired by Ebury Press (Penguin Random House) in a competitive three-way auction for UK and Commonwealth rights, according to The Bookseller. Modern Library, the Random House imprint, published it simultaneously in North America.

The memoir includes a 9,000-word foreword by Tanimoto's eldest daughter, Koko Tanimoto Kondo, now 81, who has spent 40 years campaigning for nuclear disarmament from her home in Hiroshima.

"For many years I could not live in Hiroshima, the city of my birth. On the day the atomic bomb dropped I was eight months old, a baby in the arms of my mother. It was 40 years before she could bring herself to tell me, in her own words, how I had survived."

— Koko Tanimoto Kondo, foreword to "Hiroshima, 8:15"

A Film in the Works

The memoir is also being adapted into a feature film. Japanese actor Takehiro Hira, known for his role in Netflix's "Giri/Haji," will play Tanimoto. Producer Donald Rosenfeld, former president of Merchant Ivory Productions, said pre-production begins in November with filming set for February 2027.

"It's an in-depth look at what this terrible bomb did," Rosenfeld told the Guardian. "It is so topical now with the Iran situation and North Korea. You can't imagine anything worse than Hiroshima, but it could be worse — supposedly 10,000 times stronger today."

Why It Still Matters

The memoir's publication arrives at a moment when nuclear tensions are elevated globally, with the Iran conflict and North Korea's arsenal keeping the issue at the forefront of international security discussions. Historians estimate that roughly 120,000 people died in the first four days after the Hiroshima bombing; three days later, a second bomb hit Nagasaki, killing approximately 73,000 more. Japan surrendered on August 15, 1945.

Tanimoto understood the stakes of forgetting. "If you can't tell this story to the world," he once told Hersey, according to the Japan Times, "we are going to die twice."

Editor Shammah Banerjee of Ebury Press said the timing felt urgent. "At this time, it feels more pressing than ever that the experience of these survivors is not forgotten but passed down the generations," she said.
